item.title: Holocene millennial climate variability influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions
item.dc:creator: Peng Zhou, Zhengguo Shi, Zhisheng An, Wenju Cai, Pascale Braconnot, Qiong Zhang
item.category: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences — matched: Antarctic, albedo, sea ice, Southern Ocean, sea surface temperature, millennial-scale, Holocene, proxy, transient simulation
A prominent unstable feature, millennial-scale climate oscillation (MCO), punctuated the Holocene. Solar activity and deep ocean variability are generally regarded as the origin of the MCO, yet the dynamics remain debated. Using a Holocene transient simulation with the EC-Earth climate model (8 to 0 ka BP), together with a global compilation of 304 temperature reconstructions, here we identify a robust ~1,350-y oscillatory mode that characterizes Holocene climate variability and is self-sustained and crucially influenced by tropical–Antarctic ocean–atmosphere interactions. Within each cycle, Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) strengthening evolves with the developing warming and an El Niño-like tropical sea surface temperature (SST) response, accompanied by anticyclonic circulation anomalies over the high-latitude Southern Ocean. Northward cold advection of the associated enhanced westerly winds off the Antarctic coast overcomes the effect of sea ice retreat to promote AABW formation, ocean stratification, and warming. Positive feedbacks including sea ice-albedo, tropical air–sea interaction, and SST-AABW magnify surface warming till AABW reaches its peak. Thereafter, reduced brine rejection from sea-ice retreat weakens AABW, counteracts the warming, and commences a switch to its cooling phase. The dominant periodicity, consistent with that inferred from proxy reconstructions, is confirmed by complementary climate simulations. These results provide an alternative physical mechanism for Holocene millennial-scale climate variability. Under future anthropogenic warming, a positive phase of the oscillation may heighten the positive feedbacks, thereby increasing the risk of rapid climate transformation.

item.title: The overshoot integral can inform climate science and policy beyond 1.5 °C of warming
item.dc:creator: James G Dyke, Jesse F. Abrams, John Schellnhuber
item.description:
Environmental Research Letters — matched: glaciology, glacier, overshoot, permafrost, Earth system, CMIP
Abstract The carbon budget framework has served as the dominant organising principle for climate science and policy, linking cumulative emissions to peak warming and providing a tractable scalar constraint for international negotiations. With 1.5 °C exceedance now imminent and virtually all mitigation scenarios involving substantial temperature overshoot before net-negative emissions could return temperatures to target, the budget framework’s utility for evaluating and minimising risk generated by warming risks becoming diminished. We propose a complementary organising principle: the overshoot integral, defined as the time-integrated temperature exceedance above a policy-relevant threshold, with units of °C·years. Analogous to degree-heating weeks in coral bleaching prediction and positive degree-days in glaciology, the overshoot integral captures both the magnitude and duration of exceedance in a single scalar quantity. Applying this metric to future climate pathways, we show that pathways with similar peak temperatures can differ by more than two orders of magnitude in their cumulative degree-year burden. Applied to CMIP7 ScenarioMIP/FaIR (Finite Amplitude Impulse Response simple climate model) trajectories, calculating overshoot integrals reveal substantial differences in cumulative thermal exposure across pathways. For Earth-system impacts whose response dynamics integrate forcing over time, spanning marine habitat, permafrost carbon and mountain glaciers, we show that cumulative thermal exposure captured by the overshoot integral contains impact-relevant information not captured by peak warming alone. A simple risk formulation combining peak and cumulative exposure improves out-of-sample prediction across all three systems. That the overshoot integral is best understood not as a reversible account that can be debited and credited, but as a cumulative dose should inform climate policy and science in the increasingly warmer future.

item.title: The uncertain impacts of an 1.5 °C overshoot-and-decline scenario on carbon stocks and productivity in terrestrial ecosystems
item.dc:creator: Laura E. Boeschoten, S J De Hertog, G Recour, Félicien Meunier, J Bitton, H Blondeel, … (+25)
item.description:
Environmental Research Letters — matched: overshoot, paleoclimate, Holocene, carbon cycle, CMIP
Abstract Overshoot scenarios, in which global temperatures peak and then decline through emission reductions and CO 2 removal, are increasingly central to climate policy as we are already approaching 1.5 °C warming. Yet the ecological reversibility of such pathways remains poorly understood, even though the trajectories of productivity and carbon stocks in terrestrial ecosystems have major implications for land-based carbon sink projections. Here we draw on four complementary lines of research to study the land carbon sink under overshoot: (i) CMIP6 models project declines in net ecosystem productivity (NEP) after peak warming. Nevertheless, NEP remains positive, leading to a stabilisation of the carbon stocks in terrestrial vegetation (cVeg). The CO 2 ramp up-down model experiment by CDRMIP underscores that these models predict near-reversibility of the vegetation carbon stock. (ii) A systematic review on global change experiments identified 256 papers (warming, drought, irrigation or elevated CO 2 , all elements of an overshoot scenario). However, only 15 included a recovery phase following treatment. This reveals a gap in experimental design for understanding ecosystem responses under overshoot conditions. Where recovery was assessed, responses were mixed, with persistent legacy effects documented after drought. (iii) Modern-day overshoot analogues, including two El Niño events and the 2018–2020 European droughts, show that compound heat and drought can cause carbon losses that recover slowly, with repeated extremes progressively reducing ecosystem resilience. (iv) Paleoclimate records from the Holocene Climatic Optimum and the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum demonstrate that exceeding ecological thresholds can trigger vegetation changes and carbon cycle feedbacks that long outlast the climatic perturbation itself. Together, these findings show that the trajectory of the terrestrial carbon sink during climate overshoot is uncertain, because ecosystem responses are often delayed, nonlinear, and threshold dependent.

item.title: EnsAI: an emulator for atmospheric ammonia ensembles
item.dc:creator: Michael Sitwell
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: data assimilation, emulator, ensemble
EnsAI is a newly developed artificial intelligence based program for efficiently generating ensembles of atmospheric surface ammonia concentrations that can be used in emissions inversions systems. Ensemble-based data assimilation methods are widely used for assimilation and emissions inversions, but are usually very computationally demanding. Once trained, EnsAI can run thousands of times faster than the physics-based models when run on graphics processing units.

item.title: 40-kyr of environmental history of the southeastern sector of paleolake Cuitzeo, central-western Mexico: Insights from abiotic and biotic proxies
item.dc:creator: Nayeli Pérez-Rodríguez, Juan Morales, Isabel Israde-Alcántara, Gabriela Domínguez-Vázquez, Miguel Ángel Cervantes-Solano, Avto Goguitchaichvili, … (+1)
item.description:
Applied Geochemistry — matched: last glacial maximum, Holocene, proxy
We present a multiproxy reconstruction of environmental changes recorded in the southeastern sector of Lake Cuitzeo (central-western Mexico) over the last ∼40 kyr. Our study integrates abiotic (major-element geochemistry, rock-magnetic parameters, pH, and electrical conductivity) and biotic proxies (diatoms and pollen) from a ∼10 m-long sedimentary core (Cz-07). This multiproxy approach provides a robust framework for identifying variations in terrigenous input, redox conditions, nutrient availability, carbonate precipitation, and hydrological balance, as well as the response of local vegetation to climate fluctuations. Comparing the Cz-07 record with previous data from a depocenter core reveals some spatial differences in the lake’s sensitivity to environmental changes. The sequence indicates generally low lake levels between ∼42 and ∼26.5 kyr BP, followed by pronounced environmental variability during the Last Glacial Maximum, including a marked dry episode at its onset. Enhanced runoff and predominantly oxic conditions characterize the interval from ∼17.5 to ∼11 kyr BP, encompassing the Bølling–Allerød and Younger Dryas events. During the early-to-middle Holocene (∼11.7–5 kyr BP), a progressive shift toward arid conditions is evidenced by increased carbonate precipitation, higher salinity, and reduced runoff. The most severe drought occurred during the middle Holocene, causing a substantial contraction of the lake’s southeastern sector. This arid phase aligns with middle Holocene drying trends reported in other lacustrine records across central Mexico.

item.title: Diversity of South China Sea Marine Heatwave Intensity Trends
item.dc:creator: Kunshan Li, Qiang Wang, Lili Zeng, Rui Shi, Bo Zhang, Fuan Xiao, … (+4)
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: heat wave
Abstract This study investigates the seasonal characteristics and physical drivers of marine heatwave (MHW) intensity trends in the South China Sea (SCS) during 1993–2022. Results reveal a robust, seasonally consistent north-south divergent pattern: MHW intensity has intensified pronouncedly in the northern and northwestern SCS while declining on decadal timescales in the southwestern basin, forming a "rich-get-richer, poor-get-poorer" contrast. Mixed-layer heat budget diagnostics show that enhanced net surface heat flux (Qnet), driven by increased shortwave radiation (SSR) and reduced latent heat loss, primarily causes MHW intensification in the northern and northwestern SCS. In contrast, changes in the South China Sea West Boundary Current (SCS WBC) dominate in the southwestern SCS, where a weakening northward WBC in summer and strengthening southward WBC in winter shift horizontal advection toward net cooling, and thereby weakens MHWs. Teleconnection analyses link this regional disparity to different large-scale climate modes across seasons. Strengthening of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) respectively increase SSR over the northern SCS during summer and winter, while the negative phase shift of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) and ENSO weakens anticyclonic forcing that modulates the SCS WBC in the southwestern SCS in both seasons. These findings highlight the importance of seasonal and regional heterogeneity in MHW dynamics for improving the prediction of extreme ocean warming in marginal seas.

item.title: Linking rain-on-snow events to river floods in the Tianshan Mountains
item.dc:creator: Fan Sun, Ross Woods, Xingming Hao, Yupeng Li, Gonghuan Fang, Qixiang Liang, … (+3)
item.description:
Weather and Climate Extremes — matched: cryosphere, snowpack, reanalysis
Rain-on-snow (ROS) events are widely recognized as an important cryosphere–hydrology coupling mechanism, yet when and where ROS events translate into river floods remains poorly constrained, particularly in arid high-mountain regions. Here, we provide the first basin-scale assessment of potential flood-inducing ROS (ROS-PF) and actual river-flood-generating ROS (ROS-AF) events across the Tianshan Mountains. Using ERA5-Land reanalysis (1951–2019) and an observation-based reconstructed daily streamflow dataset covering 40 Tianshan watersheds, we link ROS forcing to reconstructed high-flow responses. ROS-PF events—defined by rainfall ≥10 mm occurring on snowpack with snow water equivalent ≥10 mm—are concentrated in spring (April–June) and mid-elevations (2.0–3.5 km), within a narrow temperature window of–0.24 ± 1.49 °C. Their frequency has increased significantly over the past seven decades, driven primarily by rising heavy rainfall occurrence rather than snow availability. On average, ROS-PF events contributed on average 14.7% of the 6-day snowmelt total and 8.3% of the 6-day available-water total across the Tianshan basins. Crucially, only ∼44% of ROS-PF events evolve into ROS-AF events, revealing strong basin-dependent conversion efficiency. Some basins like Pochengzi basin convert nearly all ROS-PF events into floods, while others exhibit high ROS-PF frequency but minimal flood response. Most ROS-AF events occur with a lag of up to six days, underscoring the importance of delayed hydrological responses. These findings demonstrate that ROS does not uniformly amplify flood risk but instead reorganizes flood-generation pathways under warming, with implications for flood forecasting and water management in arid mountain systems.

item.title: Prediction-Constrained Multimodal Temporal Fusion of Satellite Microwave and Infrared Observations for Continuous Snow Temperature Profile Estimation
item.dc:creator: Zhiwei Chen, Yujie Tan, Wenchao Zheng, Yuhang Huang
item.description:
Applied Sciences — matched: Antarctic, snowpack, remote sensing
Snow temperature profiles are important for characterizing snowpack thermal state and vertical heat transfer, but continuous estimation is limited by sparse in situ observations and discrete satellite overpasses. This study proposes a prediction-constrained multimodal temporal fusion method combining continuous deep-learning prediction with satellite microwave–infrared updates. The Weather-Forced Residual LSTM with Persistence Fallback (WFRL-P) generates an hourly multi-depth prediction background from historical snow temperatures and meteorological forcing. Snow temperature profiles are then conjointly retrieved from AMSR2 microwave and MODIS infrared brightness temperatures, and valid retrieval–prediction differences are transformed into depth-dependent, magnitude-limited updates and causally propagated for up to 6 h. Independent evaluation at Dome C during 2020–2021 produced hourly estimates at 12 depths from 5 to 1000 cm, with an all-depth bias of −0.1263 K, MAE of 0.3657 K, RMSE of 0.8218 K, and R2 of 0.9880. At most comparable depths, the estimation errors were lower than those reported in previous Antarctic snow temperature remote-sensing studies. Multimodal fusion further reduced the all-depth MAE of the fixed lead-24 prediction background by 3.32%, with a 5.14% improvement at matched satellite-overpass samples. The results demonstrate that satellite microwave and infrared observations can provide effective incremental constraints while maintaining the overall accuracy of the continuous prediction background, offering a feasible approach for the temporal fusion of discrete satellite observations and continuous snow temperature predictions.

item.title: Snow and Ice Cover Change in the Earth's Third Pole: Implications for Future Water Resources
item.dc:creator: Fred Deng
item.description:
Applied and Computational Engineering — matched: glacier, meltwater, climate change
The Tibetan Plateau, Earth's "Third Pole," holds critical glacial water reserves that sustain billions of people across Asia. Climate change drives widespread glacier retreat across the region, but melt rates vary sharply by location, creating a need for fine-scale local monitoring to support adaptive water management. This study quantifies annual late-summer changes in snow and ice cover in a 100 × 125 mile central Himalayan study area near Mount Everest, using Landsat 8 satellite imagery processed in Google Earth Engine with the Normalized Difference Snow Index. Year-to-year changes were measured via image subtraction for 13 intervals from 2013 to 2026, and linear regression with a t-test was used to evaluate long-term trends. Results show net annual snow and ice loss across all 13 year-to-year intervals, although the magnitude of loss varies widely from year to year. A slight negative trend in annual loss was not statistically significant (p = 0.458), indicating no clear statistically significant long-term change in the annual loss trend over the study period. These local findings complement regional assessments and support targeted water resource planning for communities dependent on Third Pole meltwater.

item.title: A global eddy-collocated temperature and salinity profile dataset (v1.0): integrating multiplatform in situ observations with satellite-tracking mesoscale eddies
item.dc:creator: Qingyou He, Yunchen Liu, Weikang Zhan, Yinghui He, Zhenting Mo, Peiya Zhang, … (+3)

Earth System Science Data — matched: extreme event, climate change
We integrated nearly 30 years of global ocean temperature and salinity profile data with satellite mesoscale eddy observations, matching 5.46 million in-situ profiles to adjacent eddies. This dataset enables researchers to characterize the regional three-dimensional eddy structure and investigate how eddies modify ocean thermohaline distributions, alter stratification and mixing, trigger extreme events, drive heat and tracer transport, and respond to climate change.

item.title: Rainy Season Onset in Central America and the Influence of the ENSO Decaying Phase
item.dc:creator: Alan A. García‐López, Ángel G. Muñoz, Richard Seager, Ron. L. Miller
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: sea surface temperature, sea level
Abstract The description and understanding of physical mechanisms related to delayed rainy season onset in Central America can provide a framework for early warning systems based on a combination of sub-seasonal and seasonal forecasts. This is especially important in regions affected by recurrent rainfall deficits, such as the Central American Dry Corridor. Here, a generalized approach is presented to compute the onset of the rainy season and to analyze physical drivers and their intraseasonal evolution. The independent and joint influences of both the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and the sea-surface temperature of the Tropical North Atlantic (TNA) are discussed by analyzing high-resolution daily rainfall data, moist static stability, vertically-integrated moisture convergence, low-level winds and sea level pressure anomalies for the period 1981–2022. Strongly delayed onsets (more than 7 days) occur over northern Central America in the boreal spring following the peak of El Niño events driven by tropospheric warming due to El Niño, whereas La Niña events tend to modestly hasten the onset due to tropospheric cooling. However, certain regions in northern Central America still experience delays during La Niña. In addition, La Niña events with a warm TNA show significantly delayed onset over the Caribbean side of northern Central America. In this case, onset delay is related to a reduction in surface moisture due to an anomalous low-level circulation likely induced by an extratropical wave-train but not by TNA warming. The results suggest that it is key to consider Pacific-Atlantic basin interactions and their impact on the mid-troposphere when diagnosing rainfall characteristics and rainy season onset in Central America.
